query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloy (HEA) strength and hardness are primarily governed by lattice distortion from the random distribution of dissimilarly sized atoms, which impedes dislocation motion. This effect is further enhanced when controlled heat treatments induce uniform, coherent nanoprecipitates that act as additional dislocation pinning sites.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic HEA (e.g., in FCC or BCC single‐solid solution form) with a homogeneous microstructure and minimal secondary phases.
generation.intervention: Adjust the alloy design by varying the constituent elements to create two variants—one with large atomic size differences (high lattice distortion) and another with similar atomic sizes (low lattice distortion). In addition, apply controlled heat treatments to one variant to promote the formation of coherent nanoprecipitates.
generation.conditions: Testing conducted at room temperature to moderate elevated temperatures (up to about 400°C) where dislocation-mediated plastic deformation dominates. All samples should be processed under identical conditions apart from the designed compositional and heat treatment differences.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and uniformly distributed coherent nanoprecipitates that interact with dislocations.
generation.mechanism: The random mixing of elements with different atomic radii creates severe local strain (lattice distortion), increasing the energy barrier for dislocation movement (solid solution strengthening). When coherent nanoprecipitates form, they further obstruct dislocation glide, enhancing yield strength and hardness via precipitation hardening.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEAs with high atomic size mismatch and/or a high density of coherent nanoprecipitates will show significantly increased hardness and yield strength relative to the baseline (low distortion, single‐phase) alloy; measured properties should scale with the degree of atomic misfit and precipitate volume fraction.
generation.baseline: An HEA composed of elements with similar atomic radii (minimizing lattice distortion) and processed to maintain a single-phase, homogeneous structure without precipitate reinforcement.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold under conditions where dislocation motion dominates (room temperature to moderate elevated temperatures) and the alloy’s microstructure remains stable (without excessive phase segregation or formation of brittle intermetallic compounds). It may not apply if high temperature or processing conditions lead to grain boundary–dominated deformation or significant microstructural instability.
generation.uncertainty: The relative quantitative contributions of lattice distortion versus coherent nanoprecipitate strengthening remain uncertain and may vary across different HEA systems and processing routes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with a high atomic size mismatch alloy designed to maximize lattice distortion (with or without additional heat treatment to form coherent nanoprecipitates) and one baseline alloy with elements of similar atomic size. Ensure identical processing and microstructural homogeneity except for the intentional compositional differences. Perform mechanical testing (hardness and tensile tests) and use microscopy (TEM/SEM) and XRD to characterize microstructure and phase content.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and stress-strain behavior
TEM/SEM imaging to assess lattice distortions and precipitate distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high lattice distortion (or precipitate-strengthened) alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in hardness and yield strength compared to the baseline alloy, or if microstructural analyses reveal no correlation between lattice distortion/precipitates and dislocation pinning, then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

Although a lack of HEA phase diagrams limit the availability of thermodynamic data, some thermodynamic properties, such as atomic size, melting point, mixing entropy, mixing enthalpy, and valence electron concentration, can be used as criteria to predict the phase formation in the HEA system. According to the empirical rules, BCC solid solutions were generally formed in HEA systems under the following certain conditions. Chen et al. [ [13] ]. Guo et al. [ [28] ] further proposed that all ductile alloys have a VEC ≤ 4.4, while all brittle alloys have a VEC ≥ 4.6. Therefore, the NbMoCrTiAl RHEA should be without ductility and it is indeed a type of brittle RHEA.
